Ok, but "eat less, move more" really is all there is to it. Easier said than done, yes, but it's that simple. There are a million diets and fitness regimes, and they all amount to those four little words. Do you want to lose weight? Really lose weight? Do this. Find a Bmi calculator online. this will help you calculate how many caries your body physically, literally needs to maintain your current weight. Eat anything less than that and you will lose weight, guaranteed. If your body requires 3000 calories to maintain your current weight, reduce your daily intake by 5000 calories and you will lose approximately one pound a week. 500 calories is one less soda and three less slices of bread. Combine this with walking and you'll be on fire. Watch the weight come off week by week. Watch how much easier it gets to walk, how much better you feel and look. Make changes to your diet that you can live with. Don't say you'll never drink soda again. Or you'll never eat a candy bar again. Or no more carbs. Make changes that you can live with the rest of your life. Myfitnesspal is a great little app for tracking calories, THE key to weight loss. Excersise is great, but without a proper diet, it's useless.

I use MFP myself. Other people find success with sparkpeople. I find the hardest part is tracking accurately and being honest with yourself. The fudge factor gets a bunch of people. Everybody miscalculates and needs to reevaluate what they're doing.

However, diet (not dieting, but diet, what you eat) is the number one biggest factor in weight loss by like 80%.

Absolutely diet vs dieting. You gotta make life changes. It helps to recognize food as energy that your body needs to survive, rather than something for your senses to indulge in. My breakfast, almost daily, is two scrambled eggs with a side of meat, totaling less than 300 calories. It tastes good, and it keeps me going til lunch. I only drink water. If I were to add toast, that would be an additional 150 calories. Potatoes, another 150. Milk or arrange juice, you get the picture. In addition to the added calories, my cravings explode when I have bread or sugary drinks. It's much easier for me to abstain than to resist the temptation to over eat.

I need to lose weight, but I know that I would never stick to a diet. Any time I have tried, it's like a part of my brain takes over and turns my cravings into obsessions. So one day I realized I needed to stop focussing on what I shouldn't eat, and instead just started increasing what I should eat. Putting more and more vegetables on the plate pushed out a lot of the extra carbs and over time, I've gotten to love some of the healthy options. Also..l drank a lot of milk but switched out to water for the most part. I really notice when I slide back on that one. Oh...and when I have a nice glass of wine or a beer, I put out cheese, olives, maybe some hummus and only a few naan crisps or other small crackers. No chips and trying to avoid the baguettes. I will be moving the crackers into carrots and other veggies next.

So my contribution would be....stay focused on the positive! Add the good things! Don't deny yourself tasty things, just slowly start substituting them!

Next step for me is to get more exercise. It's tough to fit it on to a busy schedule, but my son just moved back after university and both of us like to ride bikes, so that will start on the weekend. It's easy to get in a good ride in under 1/2 hour on those busy nights.

I had a good bike ride just last night. Definitely a good low impact, high intensity(if you push) workout.

Good for you about finding a diet that works. If it ever stops feel free to ask for advice. Diet is number one for weight loss.

So, first, here's my /v/introductions post that has the short and sweet version: https://voat.co/v/introductions/comments/101658

For you, I'll post the sordid details, as I understand them.

PS I just finished and came back here to say I'm sorry, it turned into a novel, and that's not what I intended but I got carried away.

THE BEGINNING

So, when I was nine years old, I was a grade A jackass. Mean spirited, spiteful, bullying, the whole bit. Not, like, psychopathic, but I was just a total dick.

I had a younger sister and a younger brother, and another sister on the way. The day she was born, everybody piled into our shitty family van that was falling apart at every place it could fall apart, and headed to the hospital.

I did not take sitting in a waiting room well. Yes, I was enough of a dick that I decided to mess around inside a damn hospital.

Anyway, I don't even remember what happened, but I got grounded for it.

The next day, I began displaying flu-like symptoms.

A week later, I could not move off of my bed because I was in excruciating pain. And I do mean excruciating.

The next day, I was flown to Denver Children's Hospital in a helicopter. Even in my haze, I knew that was wicked cool.

A day after that, my parents were told that I would die. I wasn't told this until I was sixteen.

Three days after that, one Dr. Manco-Johnson took over my case. Brilliant, brilliant hematologist.

Two months later, I woke up in less excruciating pain, having been effectively comatose that whole time.

WHAT HAPPENED (yes that whole part you just read was exposition)

So during the two months of being a comatose 9 yr old, Dr. Manco-Johnson discovered that the problem lay in my immune system, which was damn near a death sentence at my age.

By the backhanded grace of god, she had followed a case almost identical to mine nearly five years earlier. Unfortunately, that case ended with the death of a little girl.

Because of that, they now knew precisely what wouldn't work, and that was one of a million vital factors in saving my life.

So they put me on chemotherapy. No, I didn't have cancer. This was to weaken my immune system enough that they could give me anticoagulants that would be effective.

They doubted I would live, which I am sure is why they were willing to do some of the things that they did. "This guy won't live, but may as well extract as much data as possible." Again, one of a million things that saved my life.

Anyway, they put nets, coils, little metal wires in major arteries whose purpose was to hopefully catch any clots that were trying to make it to more vital areas, like the brain or heart. They dumped anticoagulants into me like it was going out of style. I was a science experiment, and I am so, so glad to have been one.

You see, this was the way to develop the super soldier serum. Hahahaa I'm just kidding

WHAT HAPPENED THEN (I hope this all fits into one comment)

From what the docs tell me, the flu-like symptoms in the beginning were probably just the flu. It was just a one in a million chance that my immune system freaked out.

So anyway, the important part for me is that I was filled to the brim with blood clots. The most notable one was a huge clot that completely obstructed blood flow to the left lung via the left pulmonary artery. This mean that my left lung was completely useless, and lost to me. At least until we find a way to cure my blood disorder, which is antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

If you want to do a bit of research, you'll find that adults have consistently survived this since the nineties. Kids? It's rare in kids. But they only started surviving APAS since The Human Pincushion here made his debut.

That's a joke, by the way; it had nothing to do with me and everything to do with Dr. Manco-Johnson and her team. I was literally just laying there unconscious for just about all of it. Her research has saved dozens of children's lives.

And she wouldn't even have been able to save me if it weren't for the girl she'd followed a few years earlier. If that kid and me were reversed, it'd be her who lived. Maybe. There were a lot of maybes that happened to land on my side.

A few years after the whole losing my lung thing (which did wonders to mellow me out, btw), and after I became an angst ridden, bitch ass little shit of a teenager, I started feeling the effects of only having one lung available to me. Chest pains. Palpitating heartbeats. Fainting spells.

Finally I was diagnosed with stage 3b heart failure. For those who don't know what this means, here is a link to the classes of heart failure:

http://www.heart.org/HEARTORG/Conditions/HeartFailure/AboutHeartFailure/Classes-of-Heart-Failure_UCM_306328_Article.jsp#mainContent
